meta.blurb: Sink from the bright surface to the darkest trench and meet the animals that glow, hunt and wander there. This is a journey through the largest living space on Earth, and a look at why it needs our care.
meta.bible: The reader is the traveller: the book is a journey downward from the surface of the sea to the deepest trench, then outward across the whole world ocean, and then home. Oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic, which are really one connected body of water; it covers about seventy-one percent of Earth. Zones: Sunlight zone (to about two hundred metres), Twilight zone (about two hundred to one thousand metres), Midnight zone (below one thousand metres). Life: Plankton, Phytoplankton (tiny floating plants), Zooplankton (tiny floating animals), Krill, Baleen (the strainer in some whales' mouths), Blue whale, Sperm whale, Humpback whale, Dolphin, Shark, Turtle, Coral, Reef, Polyp, Kelp, Otter, Mangrove, Anglerfish, Squid, Eel, Tube worms, Bacteria. Key terms: Bioluminescence (living light), Marine snow, Whale fall, Hydrothermal vent, Chemosynthesis, Current, Gulf Stream, Tide, Moon, Salt, Pressure, Oxygen, Carbon dioxide, Plastic, Bleaching, Acid. Places: Mariana Trench and its deepest point, Challenger Deep, about eleven kilometres down; the Mid-Ocean Ridge, an underwater mountain chain over sixty thousand kilometres long; the Sargasso Sea; Antarctica; Earth. People: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, who reached the bottom of Challenger Deep in the Trieste in 1960. Voice and tone: wondering, clear and calm; second person where it helps; every fact is true and numbers are marked with about; where scientists are unsure, the book says so. No gore.

B1B2: Seen from space, Earth looks blue, and the reason is the ocean. It covers about seventy-one percent of the planet, and it holds almost all of Earth's water.
Maps show five oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and the Arctic. In truth they are joined together, so one drop of water could in time travel to all of them.
Seawater is salty because rain and rivers slowly wash minerals from rocks into the sea. About three and a half parts in every hundred of seawater are salts.
On average the ocean is about three and a half kilometres deep. Under the waves there are mountains, wide plains and valleys deeper than any on land.
Our journey goes straight down, from the bright surface to the darkest floor. The deeper we go, the less light there is, and the more strange the animals become.
The top layer, called the sunlight zone, reaches down to about two hundred metres. It is bright and warm enough for plants to grow, so most ocean life lives here.
Most of the plants in the sea are far too small to see one by one. These tiny floating plants, called phytoplankton, use sunlight to make their own food.
As phytoplankton make food, they release oxygen. Scientists think they produce roughly half of all the oxygen in the air, so about every second breath you take comes from the sea.
Tiny drifting animals, called zooplankton, eat the phytoplankton. One of them is krill, a small shrimp-like animal that swims in huge swarms.
The blue whale is the largest animal known ever to have lived, and it is about thirty metres long. Strangely, it feeds mainly on krill, the tiny animals we have just met.
Whales like the blue whale have no teeth. Instead, they have long plates of baleen in their mouths, which work like a comb and strain krill from the water.
Dolphins hunt in groups, and they are clever at working together. Each bottlenose dolphin has its own special whistle, which seems to work like a name.
Sharks have swum in the sea for more than four hundred million years, which is older than trees. They can smell tiny amounts of blood and sense the weak electric signals of other animals.
Sea turtles swim thousands of kilometres across the ocean. Years later, the females return to lay eggs on the same beach where they were born, perhaps by sensing the Earth's magnetic field.
Coral reefs grow in warm, shallow water and are often called the rainforests of the sea. They cover less than one percent of the sea floor, yet about a quarter of ocean species live in or near them.
Corals are not plants or rocks, but animals called polyps, which build hard skeletons around themselves. Tiny algae live inside them, and they share food in exchange for a safe home.
In cold, clear water, giant kelp grows in tall underwater forests. It can grow more than half a metre in a single day and gives food and shelter to fish, otters and many other animals.
The Moon's gravity pulls on the ocean and creates the tides. In most places the water rises and falls twice a day, and many animals live in the pools it leaves behind.
Most waves are made by the wind blowing across the sea. A wave carries energy across the ocean, but the water itself mostly moves up and down in small circles.
Winds and the spinning Earth push the surface water around the world in great currents. The Gulf Stream, for example, carries warm water north across the Atlantic and keeps parts of Europe milder.
Near the poles, very cold salty water becomes heavy and sinks. It then creeps along the sea floor, and one full trip around the world can take hundreds of years.
The ocean works like a giant sponge for heat. It has taken in most of the extra heat from global warming, and it absorbs roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide that people release.
Below about two hundred metres, we enter the twilight zone. Here only a faint blue light remains, and it fades completely by about one thousand metres.
Every night, vast numbers of twilight animals swim up towards the surface to feed in the dark. At dawn they sink back down again, in what may be the largest migration on Earth.
In the dark, a great many animals make their own light, using a chemical reaction in their bodies. This living light is called bioluminescence.
Some animals use light as a disguise. They glow gently from their undersides, so that from below they match the faint light from above and leave no shadow.
Below about one thousand metres is the midnight zone. There is no sunlight at all, the water is only a few degrees above freezing, and the pressure is crushing.
The deeper you go, the harder the water presses on everything. Deep-sea animals survive because their bodies are soft and mostly full of water, with no air spaces to be squashed.
The anglerfish waits in the dark, dangling a glowing lure above its huge mouth. Small animals swim toward the light, and the fish snaps them up.
Sperm whales can dive more than a kilometre deep and stay down for over an hour to hunt squid. The giant squid, their famous prey, was filmed alive in the deep sea only in 2012.
Dead plankton, bits of animals and waste fall through the water like slow snow. This marine snow is the main food for many animals in the dark, which take weeks to receive it.
When a large whale dies, its body sinks to the sea floor. It becomes a whale fall, which can feed a whole community of animals for many years.
The longest mountain chain on Earth is hidden under the sea. This Mid-Ocean Ridge runs for more than sixty thousand kilometres, and new sea floor is made along it.
In 1977, scientists exploring the deep sea found hot springs on the sea floor, called hydrothermal vents. To their surprise, the place was full of life.
There is no sunlight at the vents, so how can anything live? Bacteria use chemicals from the hot water to make food, and they feed animals such as tube worms.
Water at some vents is hotter than three hundred degrees Celsius. It does not turn to steam, because the weight of the water above holds it down.
The deepest place in the ocean is the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, almost eleven kilometres down. In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached it in a ship called the Trieste.
Even at the very bottom of the deepest trench, life goes on. Small shrimp-like animals live there, and so do sea cucumbers, which feed on the marine snow that falls from above.
Sound travels much farther in water than in air. Whales use songs, clicks and calls to talk to each other, and toothed whales use clicks to find food by echo.
Many whales make very long yearly journeys. Humpbacks swim thousands of kilometres from cold feeding waters to warm waters where their calves are born.
European eels live in rivers, but they are believed to swim across the Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea to breed. Scientists have found the tiny young there, but nobody has ever seen the adults breed.
The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica and is very cold, yet it is rich in life. Krill gather there in huge numbers and feed penguins, seals and whales.
We have mapped much less of the sea floor in detail than of the land. Scientists also think that many ocean species have not yet been discovered or named.
Fish are food for billions of people, but we sometimes catch them too quickly. More than a third of the world's fish stocks are fished faster than they can recover.
Millions of tonnes of plastic rubbish reach the sea every year. Animals eat it or become tangled in it, and tiny pieces have been found from the surface to the deepest trench.

When the water becomes too warm, corals lose their algae and turn white, which is called bleaching. More carbon dioxide also makes the sea slightly more acid, which makes it harder for shellfish to build their shells.
There is good news, too. After commercial whaling was stopped or limited, many whale populations, including humpbacks in many places, have begun to recover.
When part of the sea is well protected, fish usually grow bigger and become more numerous there. Some fish may even spread to nearby waters, where fishers can catch them.
Each of us can help the ocean. We can choose seafood that is caught in a sustainable way, use less plastic, and support those who work to protect the sea.
The ocean connects everyone on Earth, whether they live by the sea or far from it. It gives us oxygen, food and a stable climate, and in return it deserves our wonder and our care.
C1C2: Seen from space, our planet is not green or brown but a deep and shining blue, and the reason is the ocean. It covers about seventy-one percent of the surface and holds roughly ninety-seven percent of all the water on Earth. This book is an invitation to sink slowly beneath that surface, and to discover the largest living space our world has to offer.

On our maps the ocean is divided into five named parts, the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and the Arctic, and the Pacific alone is larger than all the land on Earth put together. These divisions are a convenience for people, however, because the water moves freely from one to the next. A single drop could, given enough time, visit every one of them.

The sea is salty because, over a vast span of time, rain and rivers have washed minerals out of the rocks and carried them downhill into the ocean, where they remain. When water evaporates, the salt stays behind, and today about three and a half parts in every hundred of seawater are dissolved salts. That is why the ocean is not a drink for any thirsty traveller.

The ocean is far deeper than most people imagine, with an average depth of about three and a half kilometres, and in places the floor falls away to nearly eleven. Beneath the waves lie mountain ranges, wide flat plains and valleys far deeper than any canyon on land. It is a landscape on a grand scale, hidden entirely under a roof of water.

Our journey will run in a straight line downward, from the glittering surface to the darkest floor of the sea. With every hundred metres the light will fade, the cold will deepen and the pressure will build, and the creatures we meet will grow stranger and more inventive. Scientists divide this long descent into three great layers, and we shall visit each of them in turn.

The first layer, called the sunlight zone, extends from the surface to a depth of about two hundred metres, and it is here that the sea is brightest and warmest. Because enough light reaches it for plants to grow, this thin upper skin supports most of the life in the ocean. Everything below it, in one way or another, depends on what happens up here.

Most of the plants in the sea are so small that you could not pick out a single one with the naked eye. These drifting cells, called phytoplankton, use sunlight and dissolved minerals to make their own food, just as the leaves of a tree do on land. Together they make up the great invisible meadow upon which the whole upper ocean grazes.

As phytoplankton make their food, they release oxygen as a waste product, and the amount is astonishing. Scientists estimate that they produce roughly half of all the oxygen on Earth, so that about one breath in every two that you take can be traced to the sea. Few people ever think to thank a speck of green that is invisible to them.

Tiny drifting animals, known collectively as zooplankton, graze on the phytoplankton, and among them are the krill, small shrimp-like creatures that gather in swarms of astonishing size. Each swarm is a mobile larder, and almost every larger animal nearby is eager to eat from it. In this way, sunlight caught by a microscopic plant is passed on, link by link, up a very long chain.

The blue whale, which can reach about thirty metres in length, is the largest animal known ever to have lived, larger even than the biggest dinosaurs. Yet this enormous creature feeds mainly on krill, which are no longer than a finger, and during the feeding season it may swallow millions of them every day. It is a remarkable proof that a very small meal, taken often enough, can build a giant.

Whales of this kind have no teeth at all, but instead carry long fringed plates of baleen that hang from the upper jaw like the teeth of an enormous comb. A whale takes in a huge mouthful of water and swarming krill, pushes the water out through the plates, and swallows the food that is left behind. It is the largest filter ever to have swum in the sea.

Dolphins are fast, social hunters that work together to herd fish into tight balls where they are easy to catch. Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, which other dolphins seem to use rather like a name when they call to one another. Scientists are still learning how much meaning these sounds carry, but the evidence for real communication keeps growing.

Sharks have been swimming in the oceans for more than four hundred million years, a span that makes them older than trees and far older than the dinosaurs. Their senses are extraordinary, for they can detect a very faint scent in the water and even the weak electric signals that every living animal gives off. Despite their reputation, only a small number of the many species are dangerous to people.

A young sea turtle crawls down a beach into the surf and vanishes into the ocean, where it may travel thousands of kilometres over many years. Remarkably, the adult females return to lay their eggs on the very beach where they were born, and scientists believe they may find it with the help of the Earth's magnetic field. How they do it so exactly is not yet fully understood.

In warm, shallow and clear water, coral reefs rise like underwater cities, and they are often called the rainforests of the sea. They cover less than one percent of the sea floor, yet roughly a quarter of all known marine species depend on them for food or shelter. The crowding of life into so small a space is one of the great wonders of the natural world.

A coral may look like a stone or a flower, yet it is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, each of which builds a hard skeleton of limestone around itself. Inside their tissues live microscopic algae that capture sunlight and share the food they make, in return for a safe place to live. Over thousands of years, the stony skeletons pile up to make an entire reef.

In cool, clear coastal waters, giant kelp forms swaying forests whose tall brown fronds rise from the sea floor towards the light. In good conditions it can grow more than half a metre in a day, making it one of the fastest growing living things on Earth, and it shelters a rich community of fish, urchins and sea otters. Seen from below, the sunlight shining through is like a green and golden cathedral.

The tides are caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon, which pulls gently on the ocean and draws a great swell of water toward itself as the Earth turns. In most places the sea rises and falls twice a day, and between the two extremes lies a strip of shore where animals must survive both drowning and drying out. A rock pool at low tide is a small and crowded world.

Most ocean waves are born when wind blows across the water and pushes the surface into ripples, which then grow into swells that may travel thousands of kilometres. What moves across the sea, however, is energy and not water, since a floating bird simply rises and falls in a small circle as each wave passes beneath it. The wave arrives on the shore long after the wind that made it has gone.

Winds and the spin of the Earth drive great rivers of surface water, called currents, around the ocean basins, carrying heat from one part of the world to another. The Gulf Stream, for instance, carries warm water north across the Atlantic and helps to keep the winters of north-western Europe milder than they would otherwise be. The ocean is not a still pool but a restless and moving machine.

Near the poles, surface water becomes so cold and salty that it grows heavy and sinks, and it then creeps slowly along the deep sea floor toward the other oceans. This slow circulation, sometimes called the ocean conveyor, mixes the water of the whole planet, and a complete journey can take several hundred years or even as long as a thousand. Some of the water beneath you would then have last seen the sun long ago.

The ocean acts as a vast sponge for both heat and gas, and by doing so it has softened the effects of a warming climate on the land. It has absorbed more than ninety percent of the extra heat trapped by human activity, and it takes in roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide that we release into the air. This help, as we shall see later, does not come without a cost.

Below about two hundred metres we pass into the twilight zone, where the light is a faint and ghostly blue that grows weaker with every metre. By about one thousand metres even that last glimmer has vanished, and the temperature has fallen sharply. Plants can no longer grow here, so the animals must feed on what drifts down from above or on one another.

When night falls, an astonishing number of twilight animals, from tiny crustaceans to small fish and squid, swim upward to feed near the surface where the darkness hides them from hunters. At dawn they sink again into the depths, and this daily movement is thought to be the largest migration of animals on Earth, measured by the sheer quantity of life that takes part in it. It happens every day, and almost nobody sees it.

Down in the dimness, a great many animals produce their own light through chemical reactions inside their bodies, a talent known as bioluminescence. Some flash to confuse an attacker, some glow to attract a mate and some dangle a shining lure to bring a victim close enough to seize. On land, only a few creatures such as fireflies can do this, but in the deep sea it is almost the normal way of life.

Light can also serve as a disguise, since some animals glow softly along their undersides so as to match the faint light filtering down from above. A hunter looking up from below cannot then see the dark shape of its prey against the sky, for the shadow that would give it away has been cancelled out. It is camouflage made not of colour but of carefully chosen brightness.

Below about a thousand metres lies the midnight zone, a place where no ray of sunlight has ever arrived and where the water hovers a few degrees above freezing. This is by far the largest living space on the planet, yet its inhabitants have to live in darkness, in cold and under heavy pressure. Most of what happens here has been seen by no human eye.

Water is heavy, and the deeper one descends the more crushingly it presses on everything, until at the very bottom the pressure is more than a thousand times that at the surface. Deep-sea animals cope because their bodies are soft and filled with water, and have no pockets of air that could be flattened like an empty bottle. They are built to be at one with the pressure rather than to fight it.

The female anglerfish drifts through the darkness with a glowing lure hanging from a rod above her enormous mouth, patiently waiting for the curious. A small animal drawn toward the light comes too close, and in an instant the jaws open and close. In some species the tiny males attach themselves to a female for life, an unusual solution to the problem of finding a mate in an empty sea.

Sperm whales are the great divers of the sea, plunging more than a kilometre down and remaining below for well over an hour as they hunt for squid in the blackness. Their prey includes the giant squid, an animal so elusive that it was not filmed alive in its deep-sea home until 2012. Scars on the whales' skin hint at fierce meetings that no person has ever witnessed.

Dead plankton, fragments of animals and bits of waste are always falling from the sunlit waters above, drifting downward in a soft and endless shower that scientists call marine snow. It may take weeks to reach the sea floor, and by the time it does most of it has been eaten, but what remains feeds an astonishing number of deep-sea animals. The darkness depends entirely on a gift from the light.

When a great whale dies, its huge body may sink to the sea floor, where it becomes a feast known as a whale fall. Crabs, fish and sharks strip the flesh, and later worms and bacteria feed on the bones, so that one body can support a community of animals for many years. It is a gift of food to a place where there is very little.

The longest mountain chain on Earth is not on land at all, but is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which winds for more than sixty thousand kilometres through the ocean basins like the seam of a baseball. Along its crest, molten rock rises and cools into new sea floor, which slowly spreads sideways as the continents drift. The ocean floor is therefore far younger than the land.

In 1977, scientists exploring the sea floor near the Galápagos Islands found something that nobody had predicted: hot springs, called hydrothermal vents, pouring out mineral-rich water in the dark. Around them, to everyone's astonishment, lived a crowded community of strange animals that no one had ever seen before. It was one of the great discoveries of twentieth-century science.

Without any sunlight to power a food chain, life at the vents relies on bacteria that make food from chemicals in the hot water, a process known as chemosynthesis. These bacteria live inside tube worms, mussels and other animals, feeding their hosts in return for shelter, and whole communities have grown up on this single source of energy. It showed that life can thrive where light never comes.

At some vents the water shoots out at temperatures above three hundred degrees Celsius, far above the usual boiling point. It does not turn to steam, because the enormous pressure of the water overhead holds it as a liquid. Minerals in the hot stream turn dark as they meet the cold sea, building chimneys that smoke like small black volcanoes.

The deepest known place in the ocean is the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench of the western Pacific, which lies almost eleven kilometres below the waves. In 1960 two men, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, reached the bottom in a small steel vessel called the Trieste, and the descent took them nearly five hours. They stayed only about twenty minutes, and then they rose.

Even at the very bottom of the deepest trench, life persists, and scientists have recovered small shrimp-like animals and sea cucumbers from the muddy floor. They feed on the marine snow that funnels into the trench from above, and they thrive under a weight of water that would crush a submarine not built for it. Wherever food and water exist together, it seems, something finds a way to live.

Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, and it carries much farther, so for many ocean animals hearing is more important than sight. Humpback whales sing long and changing songs that can be heard many kilometres away, while toothed whales produce clicks and listen for the echoes to find their food. The ocean, to those who live there, is a place of voices.

Many whales make journeys of astonishing length, and the humpback is among the champions, travelling many thousands of kilometres each year between cold feeding grounds near the poles and warm waters where the calves are born. For months the mothers eat almost nothing, living on the fat they stored. It is one of the longest regular journeys of any mammal on Earth.

European eels spend years in rivers and ponds, yet when the time comes they are believed to travel thousands of kilometres across the Atlantic to breed in the Sargasso Sea. Scientists have found the tiny young eels there, but no one has ever watched the adults spawn, and exactly how they find their way remains a mystery. Even a fish we have eaten for centuries has secrets.

The Southern Ocean encircles Antarctica, and although it is bitterly cold and often stormy, it is also one of the richest seas on Earth. Krill gather beneath the ice and in the open water in vast numbers, and they feed the penguins, seals, seabirds and whales that crowd the region in summer. The ocean is cold, but it is certainly not empty.

Remarkably, much of the sea floor has still not been mapped in fine detail, and there are many parts of the ocean that no person has ever visited. Scientists think that a large number of ocean species are still unknown to science, although nobody can say exactly how many. Every expedition to the deep, as a result, has a good chance of finding something new.

Fish are an important source of food for billions of people, but modern fleets can catch them faster than they can breed. According to the United Nations, more than a third of the world's assessed fish stocks are now being fished at an unsustainable level, and some well-known species have fallen sharply. The problem is serious, though it is not hopeless, as we shall see.

Millions of tonnes of plastic waste find their way into the ocean every year, most of it carried from the land by rivers and wind. Animals mistake it for food or become tangled in it, and as it breaks into ever smaller pieces it spreads everywhere, with traces found from the surface to the deepest trench. The convenience of a moment can last in the sea for centuries.

When sea water becomes too warm, corals expel the algae that live inside them and turn a ghostly white, a process called bleaching that can kill the reef if the heat lasts too long. At the same time, the carbon dioxide absorbed by the ocean makes the water slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for shellfish and corals to build their hard skeletons. These changes are the price of the ocean's long service to the climate.

Not every story from the sea is a sad one, and the return of the whales is among the happiest. After international rules sharply limited commercial whaling, many populations, including humpbacks in many regions, began to recover, although some species remain in great danger. It shows that, given the chance, the ocean is capable of remarkable healing.

Marine protected areas, in which fishing and other damaging activities are limited or forbidden, can allow fish, corals and other animals to recover, provided the rules are real and enforced. Larger and older fish tend to return, and their young may spread to nearby waters, where they can help local fishing too. Only a small share of the ocean is well protected today, and the need for more is widely agreed.

Individuals cannot solve these problems alone, but small choices add up, particularly when many people make them at once. We can choose seafood caught in sustainable ways, use less single-use plastic, support the groups and laws that protect the sea, and speak up for the ocean wherever we can. Learning about the sea, as you have just done, is where all such actions begin.

The ocean touches every life on Earth, whether we live beside it or a thousand kilometres from the nearest shore, for it gives us oxygen, food, rain and a climate in which we can live. Its depths still hold mysteries that nobody has solved, and its health is now in human hands as never before. The journey from the bright surface to the dark trench is over, but our relationship with the sea has only just begun.
